title: Attend to milk parlour management activities

lessons.title: Organising parlour operations
lessons.html:
The parlour as a production system

The parlour is where the farm's income is harvested. A parlour manager organises people, routines and equipment so that every cow is milked fully, hygienically and calmly, within a reasonable time, and milk reaches the buyer at top quality.

Standard milking procedure

Write a standard operating procedure for the milking routine covering preparation, fore-stripping, pre-dip and contact time, drying, attachment timing, alignment, take-off settings and post-dip. Display it in the parlour in the languages of the milkers. Train every milker and assess them against it. Consistency between milkers matters as much as the routine itself.

Parlour efficiency

Measure throughput (cows per hour) and total milking time. Efficiency depends on parlour design, number of units, routine time per cow, cow flow and milker skill. Example: milking 360 cows in 2.5 hours equals 144 cows per hour. If cows wait in the collecting yard much longer than the planned time, lying time and comfort suffer, which affects yield and lameness.

Ways to improve efficiency without sacrificing quality: group cows by milking speed or production, improve cow flow with backing gates and good yard design, adjust the routine to the parlour layout, and maintain take-off settings properly.

Staffing and rosters

  • Roster milkings so that each shift has trained milkers and a person responsible.
  • Rotate tasks to prevent fatigue and repetitive strain.
  • Plan relief milkers for weekends and leave, in line with the Basic Conditions of Employment Act 75 of 1997.
  • Brief each shift on treated and problem cows.

Communication tools

Use a treatment board, cow marking system, shift handover notes and parlour logbook. Electronic ID and parlour software can flag treated cows automatically, but visual marking should remain as a backup.

lessons.title: Managing milk quality
lessons.html:
Quality targets

Set targets for bacteria count, somatic cell count, residues (zero), freezing point and tank temperature, based on the buyer's payment scheme and the code of good practice. Track results from every collection and plot trends.

Investigating a high bacteria count

Possible causeChecks
Cleaning failureWash water temperature at start and end, detergent concentration, cycle times, wash volume, air injector function, visual inspection of jars, liners and tank
Cooling failureTemperature records, time to cool, plate cooler water flow, compressor performance
Udder preparationTeat cleanliness, routine compliance, yard and bedding cleanliness
Worn rubberwareLiner age, cracked tubes, perished seals
Water qualityWater test for bacteria, treatment system working

Laboratory tests that distinguish types of bacteria, offered by some labs, can help locate the source.

Managing SCC

  • Identify high-SCC cows from milk recording or CMT.
  • Culture samples to identify pathogens.
  • Decide treatment, dry-off or culling with the vet.
  • Review milking routine, machine function and post-dip coverage.
  • Review housing, bedding and yard hygiene for environmental pathogens.

Preventing residues

Residues are the most serious quality failure. Controls include: clear marking of treated cows, a treatment board, written withdrawal dates based on labels or vet instructions, separate milking of treated cows, staff briefings, and, where useful, testing individual cows or the tank before collection. Investigate every incident and fix the system, not just the person.

Legal and contractual context

Raw milk is a foodstuff under the Foodstuffs, Cosmetics and Disinfectants Act 54 of 1972. Supply contracts set quality standards and penalties; repeated failure can lead to suspension.

lessons.title: Equipment, chemicals and parlour costs
lessons.html:
Equipment management

  • Maintenance schedule: daily operator checks, weekly checks (vacuum regulator, pump oil, belts), liner changes at the manufacturer's interval, and professional dynamic and static plant testing at the recommended interval.
  • Records: maintain a parlour equipment log with test results, repairs and parts changed.
  • Critical spares: liners, pulsators, filter socks, vacuum pump belts, so a failure does not stop milking.
  • Backup power: a generator with an automatic or well-practised manual changeover, tested regularly, so cows can be milked and milk cooled during power cuts.

Chemical management

  • Keep a chemical register and safety data sheets for detergents, acids, sanitisers and teat dips.
  • Store chemicals in a ventilated, lockable store, with acids and chlorine products separated, on bunded floors where possible.
  • Provide protective equipment: gloves, goggles, aprons, and an eyewash point.
  • Train staff on safe dilution, spill response and first aid, as the OHS Act 85 of 1993 requires employers to inform and train workers on hazards.
  • Return or dispose of empty containers as the supplier or label directs.

Parlour costs

Monitor costs per litre for parlour consumables, electricity, water, rubberware and repairs. Example: monthly parlour costs of R96 000 for 300 000 litres equals R0.32 per litre. Compare month to month and investigate spikes, such as rising electricity from a faulty cooling system or overuse of teat dip.

Environmental management

Ensure parlour waste water and spilt milk are directed into the effluent system and that the system is managed in line with the National Water Act 36 of 1998.

Evaluating parlour performance

Review monthly: milk quality results, throughput, mastitis incidence, equipment downtime, costs per litre and staff compliance with the SOP. Agree on improvements with the team.

Key points

  • Write, display and train on a standard milking SOP.
  • Measure throughput and waiting times, and protect cow comfort.
  • Investigate quality problems systematically: cleaning, cooling, preparation, rubberware, water.
  • Prevent residues with marking, records and separation.
  • Manage equipment, chemicals, backup power and costs per litre.
